title: Text Completion: one blank
lines: ## What you see on screen

A one-blank text completion shows a sentence or two with a gap, and below it five answer choices in a single column. You click one word or phrase. There is no partial credit and no penalty for guessing, so never leave an item blank.

These items test whether you can follow the logic of a sentence, not whether you have memorized a dictionary. Every correct answer is supported by a clue inside the sentence itself. Your job is to find that clue, decide what the blank must mean, and only then look at the choices.
## The four-step method

- Step 1: Cover the choices. Read the whole sentence first, ignoring the five words below it. If you read the choices first, each one will seem to fit for a moment, and you will talk yourself into a trap.
- Step 2: Find the clue. Ask: what word or phrase elsewhere in the sentence tells me about the blank? Underline it mentally.
- Step 3: Find the signal word. Ask: does the sentence continue in the same direction as the clue, or does it turn around?

- Step 4: Predict, then match. Put your own simple word in the blank (it can be plain, even clumsy), then choose the answer closest in meaning to your prediction. Reread the full sentence with your choice in it before moving on.
## Clue words: the evidence for the blank
The clue is the part of the sentence that describes the same thing the blank describes. Often it is a phrase that restates the blank, explains it, or gives an example of it.
> Although the senator was famous for long speeches, her reply to the reporter was strikingly ____: a single sentence, then silence.
> Clue: "a single sentence, then silence". Signal: "Although" (contrast with long speeches). Prediction: short, brief.
> An answer like "laconic" (using very few words) matches. "Verbose" is the opposite; "candid" (frank) is a real quality of a reply but is not what the clue describes.
Notice that the colon does a lot of work here. A colon, a semicolon, or a dash usually means that the next part explains or restates the earlier part, so whatever follows it is a strong clue.
## Signal words: same direction or a turn
Signal words tell you how the parts of a sentence relate. Learn them in three groups.

- Contrast (the blank is opposite to the clue): although, though, but, yet, however, despite, in spite of, while, whereas, rather than, instead of, nevertheless, far from, surprisingly, paradoxically.
- Continuation or restatement (the blank agrees with the clue): and, also, moreover, in fact, indeed, that is, in other words, not only ... but also, a colon or semicolon.
- Cause and effect (the blank follows logically from the clue): because, since, so, therefore, thus, consequently, as a result, hence, given that.
> Because the new alloy proved so ____, engineers could bend it into tight curves without any cracks forming.
> Clue: bend into tight curves without cracks. Signal: "Because" (cause). Prediction: flexible.
> "Malleable" or "pliant" fits; "brittle" is the reverse; "durable" sounds positive and technical but does not explain the bending.
> The critic, far from dismissing the debut novel, called it ____ and urged readers to seek it out.

> Signal: "far from dismissing" (a turn away from negativity). Second clue: "urged readers to seek it out". Prediction: excellent, praiseworthy. "Laudable" works; "pedestrian" (ordinary, dull) is the trap for anyone who missed the turn.

! Some sentences have no signal word at all. Then the relationship is usually restatement: the blank and the clue describe the same thing. Ask yourself what the sentence would say if you removed the blank.
## Charge and degree: two quick filters
Before you even settle on a precise prediction, decide the blank's charge: is it positive or negative? This alone often removes two or three choices.
Then think about degree: how strong must the word be? The GRE likes to offer one choice with the right charge but the wrong strength.
> The board expected mild objections to the merger; instead, shareholders were ____, flooding the meeting with angry letters and threats to sell.
> Charge: negative. Degree: strong, because "instead" contrasts with "mild" and the clue mentions a flood of angry letters.
> "Irate" or "incensed" fits. "Disappointed" has the right charge but is far too mild, so it fails the degree test.
> The results were only ____ encouraging: the drug helped a few patients slightly, while most saw no change.
> Degree words such as "only", "somewhat", "hardly" and "scarcely" shape the blank. Prediction: slightly, modestly. "Marginally" fits; "overwhelmingly" has the right direction but the wrong degree.
## Predicting when the choices are hard words

Your prediction does not need to be sophisticated. If you predict "stubborn", you can still match it to "obdurate" or "intransigent". When you do not know a choice, do not pick it simply because it looks impressive, and do not rule it out simply because it is unfamiliar. Eliminate the words you know are wrong; if one unknown word remains, it is often right.

Use word roots carefully. "Equivocal" contains "equi" (equal) and "voc" (voice), which hints at speaking with two equal voices, that is, being ambiguous. Roots can mislead, though, so treat them as a tiebreaker rather than proof.
> The witness's testimony was so ____ that each lawyer claimed it supported her own client.

> Clue: both sides could read it their way. Prediction: unclear, two-sided. "Equivocal" fits; "emphatic" is the reverse; "lengthy" is a real feature of testimony but does not explain why both sides benefit.
## Traps the GRE sets

! The opposite trap: a word that means the exact reverse of the correct answer. It catches readers who miss a contrast signal such as "although" or "far from". Always mark the signal before predicting.

! The topic trap: a word associated with the subject of the sentence (a legal word in a sentence about a trial, a scientific word in a sentence about a lab) that does not match the clue. Relevance to the topic is not evidence.
! The degree trap: the right idea at the wrong strength. "Annoyed" for "furious", "liked" for "revered".

! The second-meaning trap: the GRE often uses common words in less common senses. "Qualified" can mean limited ("qualified approval"), "check" can mean restrain, and "temper" can mean moderate. If a simple word seems to fit oddly, test its second meaning.
! The double-negative trap: phrases such as "not unwilling" or "hardly lacking in" flip twice. Translate them into plain positive language before predicting: "not unwilling" means willing.
## A full worked example
> Mitigation efforts did not eliminate the flood risk, but they did ____ it: damage in the following storm was roughly half that of the previous one.

> Step 1: Read without choices. Step 2: The clue is "damage ... roughly half". Step 3: "did not eliminate ... but they did" signals a partial success, a turn from total to partial. Step 4: Predict "reduce".
> Suppose the choices are: exacerbate, abate, eradicate, document, forecast.

> "Exacerbate" (make worse) is the opposite trap. "Eradicate" (wipe out) is the degree trap, since the sentence says the risk was not eliminated. "Document" and "forecast" are topic words linked to storms and risk, but they do not mean reduce. "Abate" (lessen) matches.
## Timing

Aim for about one minute per one-blank item, and many easy ones will take only 30 to 40 seconds. The time you save here is valuable, because reading passages need longer. If you have spent 90 seconds and are still torn between two choices, pick the one closer to your prediction, mark the item for review, and move on. You can return to marked items with the Review screen before the section ends.
## Quick checklist
- Did I read the sentence before the choices?
- What is the clue, and what is the signal (same direction, contrast, cause)?
- Is the blank positive or negative, and how strong?
- Does my choice match the prediction, and does the full sentence make sense when I reread it?
